source_text: Θέλομεν δὲ παραστῆσαι, πῶς οὐ χρησιμώτερον ἦν πρὸς τὴν οἰκονομίαν ὅλην τὸ εὐθὺς ἀπὸ τοῦ σκόλοπος αὐτὸν ἀφανῆ γενέσθαι σωματικῶς. τὰ συμβεβηκέναι ἀναγεγραμμένα τῷ Ἰησοῦ οὐκ ἐν φιλῇ τῇ λέξει καὶ τῇ ἱστορίᾳ τὴν πᾶσαν ἔχει θεωρίαν τῆς ἀληθείας· ἕκαστον γὰρ αὐτῶν καὶ σύμβολόν τινος εἶναι παρὰ τοῖς συνετώτερον ἐντυγχάνουσι τῇ γραφῇ ἀποδείκνυται. ὥσπερ οὖν τὸ σταυρωθῆναι αὐτὸν ἔχει τὴν δηλουμένην ἀλήθειαν ἐν τῷ „Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι“ καὶ τῷ σημαινομένῳ ἐκ τοῦ „ἐμοὶ δὲ μὴ γένοιτο καυχᾶσθαι εἰ μὴ ἐν τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ κυρίου μου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, δι᾿ οὗ ἐμοὶ κόσμος ἐσταύρωται κἀγὼ τῷ κόσμῳ,“ καὶ ὁ θάνατος αὐτοῦ ἀναγκαῖος διὰ τὸ „ὃ γὰρ ἀπέθανε, τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀπέθανεν ἐφάπαξ“ καὶ διὰ τὸ τὸν δίκαιον λέγειν· „συμμορφιζόμενος τῷ θανάτῳ αὐτοῦ“ καὶ τὸ „εἰ γὰρ (συν) απεθάνομεν, καὶ συζήσομεν“· οὕτως καὶ ἡ ταφὴ αὐτοῦ φθάνει ἐπὶ τοὺς συμμόρφους τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ καὶ τοὺς συσταυρωθέντας αὐτῷ καὶ συναποθανόντας, καθὸ καὶ τῷ Παύλῳ λέλεκται τό· „συνετάφημεν γὰρ αὐτῷ διὰ τοῦ βαπτίσματος“ καὶ συνανέστημεν αὐτῷ· ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ τὰ περὶ τῆς ταφῆς καὶ τοῦ μνημείου καὶ τοῦ θάψαντος ἀναγεγραμμένα εὐκαιρότερον διὰ πλειόνων ἐν ἄλλοις. ἔνθα προηγουμένως ἔστι περὶ τούτων λέγειν, διηγησόμεθα. νυνὶ δ᾿ αὐτάρκης ἡ καθαρὰ σινδὼν, ἐν ᾗ ἔδει τὸ καθαρὸν ἐντυλιχθῆναι σῶμα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, καὶ τὸ καινὸν μνημεῖον, „ὃ ἐλατόμησε τῇ πέτρᾳ“ ὁ Ἰωσὴφ. „οὗ οὐκ ἦν οὔπω οὐδεὶς κείμενος.“ ἢ. ὡς ὁ Ἰωάννης φησὶν. „ἐν ᾧ οὐδέπω οὐδεὶς ἐτέθη.“ καὶ ἐπίστησον εἰ δύναται κινῆσαί τινα ἡ συμφωνία τῶν τριῶν εὐαγγελιστῶν, φροντισάντων ἀναγράψαι τὸ λατομητὸν ἢ λαξευτὸν μνημεῖον ἐν πέτρᾳ, ἵν᾿ ὁ τοὺς λόγους τῶν γεγραμμένων ἐξετάζων καὶ περὶ τούτων θεάσηταί τι λόγου ἄξιον καὶ περὶ τῆς καινότητος τοῦ μνημείου, ἥντινα Ματθαῖος καὶ Ἰωάννης ἱστόρησε, καὶ περὶ τοῦ μηδένα ἐκεῖ νεκρὸν γεγονέναι κατὰ τὸν Λουκᾶν καὶ τὸν Ἰωάννην. ἔδει γὰρ τὸν μὴ τοῖς λοιποῖς νεκροῖς ὅμοιον ἀλλὰ ζωτικὰ σημεῖα καὶ ἐν τῇ νεκρότητι δείξαντα τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ τὸ αἷμα καὶ καινὸν, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, ὄντα νεκρὸν ἐν καινῷ καὶ καθαρῷ γενέσθαι μνημείῳ· ἵν᾿, ὥσπερ ἡ γένεσις αὐτοῦ καθαρωτέρα πάσης γενέσεως ἦν τῷ μὴ ἀπὸ μίξεως ἀλλ᾿ ἀπὸ παρθένου γεννηθῆναι, οὕτως καὶ ἡ ταφὴ ἔχοι τὴν καθαρότητα. διὰ τοῦ συμβολικοῦ δηλουμένην ἐν τῷ ἀποτεθεῖσθαι αὐτοῦ τὸ σῶμα ἐν μνημείῳ καινῷ ὑφεστῶτι, οὐκ ἐκ λογάδων λίθων οἰκοδομηθέντι καὶ τὴν ἕνωσιν οὐ φυσικὴν ἔχοντι ἀλλ᾿ ἐν μιᾷ καὶ δι᾿ ὅλων ἡνωμένῃ πέτρᾳ λατομητῇ καὶ λαξευτῇ. τὰ μὲν οὖν τῆς διηγήσεως καὶ τῆς ἀπὸ τῶν γεγονέναι ἀναγεγραμμένων ἀναβάσεως ἐπὶ τὰ πράγματα, ὧν τὰ γενόμενα ἦν σημαντικὰ. καὶ μειζόνως ἄν τις καὶ θειοτέρως διηγήσαιτο, εὐκαιρότερον ἐκτιθέμενος τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐν προηγουμένῃ συντάξει· τὰ δὲ τῆς λέξεως καὶ οὕτως ἄν τις ἀποδῴη, ὅτι κατὰ τὸν κρίναντα ὑπομεῖναι τὸ ἐπὶ σκόλοπος κρεμασθῆναι ἦν καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς τῇ ὑποθέσει τηρῆσαι, ἵν᾿ ὡς ἄνθρωπος καθαιρεθεὶς τῷ ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἀποτεθνηκέναι ὡς ἄνθρωπος καὶ ταφῇ. ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰ καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν ἐγέγραπτο ἐν τοῖς εὐαγγελίοις ὅτι ἀπὸ τοῦ σκόλοπος ἀφανὴς εὐθὺς ἐγένετο, ἐκάκιζεν ἂν τὸ γεγραμμένον ὁ Κέλσος καὶ οἱ ἄπιστοι, καὶ κατηγόρησαν ἂν καὶ οὕτω λέγοντες· τί δή ποτε μετὰ τὸν σταυρὸν γέγονεν ἀφανὴς, οὐ πρὸ τοῦ παθεῖν δὲ τοῦτ᾿ ἐπραγματεύσατο; εἴπερ οὖν ἀπὸ τῶν εὐαγγελίων μεμαθηκότες ὅτι οὐ γέγονεν εὐθὺς ἀφανὴς ἀπὸ τοῦ σκόλοπος ἐγκαλεῖν οἴονται τῷ λόγῳ. μὴ πλασαμένῳ, ὡς ἐκεῖνοι ἠξίωσαν, τὸ εὐθὺς αὐτὸν ἀφανῆ γενέσθαι ἀπὸ τοῦ σκόλοπος ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀληθὲς ἱστορήσαντι, πῶς οὐκ εὔλογον πιστεῦσαι αὐτοὺς καὶ τῇ ἀναστάσει αὐτοῦ, καὶ ὡς βουληθεὶς ὁτὲ μὲν „τῶν θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων“ „ἔστη ἐν μέσῳ“ τῶν μαθητῶν, ὁτὲ δὲ δοὺς ἄρτον δυσὶ τῶν γνωρίμων εὐθὺς „ἄφαντος ἐγένετο ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν“ μετά τινας, οὓς ἐλάλησεν αὐτοῖς, λόγους;
pass_a_gloss: We wish to present (παραστῆσαι) how it was not more useful (χρησιμώτερον) for the whole economy (οἰκονομία) that he at once from the stake (σκόλοψ) become invisible (ἀφανής) bodily (σωματικῶς). The things written up as having happened to Jesus do not have in the bare (ψιλῇ, printed φιλῇ) wording (λέξις) and history (ἱστορία) the whole contemplation (θεωρία) of the truth; for each of them is shown (ἀποδείκνυται) also to be a symbol (σύμβολον) of something, among those who read (ἐντυγχάνουσι) the writing (γραφή) more intelligently (συνετώτερον). As then his being crucified has the truth shown (δηλουμένην) in 'I have been co-crucified (συνεσταύρωμαι) with Christ' and in what is signified (σημαινομένῳ) from 'but to me may it not be (μὴ γένοιτο) to boast (καυχᾶσθαι) except in the cross (σταυρός) of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom (δι᾿ οὗ) to me the world has been crucified and I to the world', and his death [was] necessary (ἀναγκαῖος) because of 'for what he died, he died to sin once for all (ἐφάπαξ)' and because of the righteous man saying 'being conformed (συμμορφιζόμενος) to his death' and 'for if we died with (συναπεθάνομεν), we shall also live with (συζήσομεν)'; so also his burial (ταφή) reaches (φθάνει) to those conformed (συμμόρφους) to his death and co-crucified and co-dead with him, according as (καθό) also by Paul is said: 'for we were co-buried (συνετάφημεν) with him through baptism (βάπτισμα)', and we co-rose (συνανέστημεν) with him. But we shall narrate (διηγησόμεθα) the things written about the burial and the tomb (μνημεῖον) and the one who buried (θάψαντος) more opportunely (εὐκαιρότερον) through more [words] in other [writings], where it is principally (προηγουμένως) [proper] to speak about these. But now sufficient (αὐτάρκης) [is] the clean (καθαρά) linen (σινδών), in which the clean body of Jesus had to (ἔδει) be wrapped (ἐντυλιχθῆναι), and the new (καινόν) tomb 'which Joseph hewed (ἐλατόμησε) in the rock', 'where there was not yet anyone lying (κείμενος)', or, as John says, 'in which not yet anyone was placed (ἐτέθη)'. And attend (ἐπίστησον) whether the agreement (συμφωνία) of the three evangelists can move (κινῆσαι) someone, they having taken care (φροντισάντων) to record the quarried (λατομητόν) or hewn (λαξευτόν) tomb in rock, that the one examining the reasons (λόγους) of the writings may behold (θεάσηται) about these too something worthy of account (λόγου ἄξιον), and about the newness (καινότης) of the tomb, which Matthew and John reported (ἱστόρησε), and about no corpse (νεκρός) having been there according to Luke and John. For it was necessary that the one not like the other dead, but who showed life-giving/living signs (ζωτικὰ σημεῖα) even in deadness (νεκρότης), the water and the blood, and being, so to name (ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω), a new corpse, should come to be in a new and clean tomb; that, as his birth (γένεσις) was cleaner (καθαρωτέρα) than every birth by his being born not from mixing/intercourse (μίξις) but from a virgin (παρθένος), so also the burial might have the cleanness (καθαρότης), shown through the symbolic (συμβολικόν) in his body having been laid away (ἀποτεθεῖσθαι) in a new tomb existing (ὑφεστῶτι), not built from picked stones (λογάδες λίθοι) and having union (ἕνωσις) not natural (φυσικήν), but in one rock united throughout (δι᾿ ὅλων ἡνωμένῃ), quarried and hewn. The matters of the exposition (διήγησις) and of the ascent (ἀνάβασις) from the things written as having happened to the realities (πράγματα), of which the events were signifying (σημαντικά), one might narrate more greatly (μειζόνως) and more divinely (θειοτέρως), setting out such things more opportunely in a principal treatise (προηγουμένη σύνταξις); but the things of the wording (λέξις) one might render (ἀποδῴη) also thus: that it was in keeping with the one who decided (κρίναντα) to endure (ὑπομεῖναι) being hung (κρεμασθῆναι) upon a stake also to keep (τηρῆσαι) the things following (τὰ ἑξῆς) in accord with the purpose/supposition (ὑπόθεσις), that, as a man taken down (καθαιρεθείς), by having died as a man, [he might be] also by burial as a man. But even if, by supposition (καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν), it had been written in the Gospels that from the stake he at once became invisible, Celsus and the unbelievers (ἄπιστοι) would have disparaged (ἐκάκιζεν) the writing, and would have accused also thus saying: why ever (τί δή ποτε) after the cross did he become invisible, but did not contrive (ἐπραγματεύσατο) this before suffering (παθεῖν)? If then, having learned from the Gospels that he did not at once become invisible from the stake, they think (οἴονται) to accuse (ἐγκαλεῖν) the word (λόγος) for not inventing (μὴ πλασαμένῳ), as those demanded (ἠξίωσαν), his becoming invisible at once from the stake, but reporting (ἱστορήσαντι) the true thing, how is it not reasonable (εὔλογον) that they believe also in his resurrection, and how, having willed (βουληθείς), at one time (ὁτὲ μέν) 'the doors having been shut (κεκλεισμένων)' he 'stood in the middle' of the disciples, at another (ὁτὲ δέ) having given bread to two of his acquaintances (γνώριμοι) at once 'became unseen (ἄφαντος) from them' after certain words which he spoke to them?
pass_b_english: We wish to show how it would not have been more useful for the whole dispensation that he should vanish bodily from the stake at once. The things recorded as having happened to Jesus do not hold the whole contemplation of the truth in the bare wording and the history. For each of them is shown, to those who read Scripture with more understanding, to be also a symbol of something.

His crucifixion holds the truth made plain in “I have been crucified with Christ” (Galatians 2:20), and in what is meant by “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14). His death was necessary because of the words “For the death he died, he died to sin once for all” (Romans 6:10), and because the righteous man says “being conformed to his death” (Philippians 3:10), and “For if we have died with him, we shall also live with him” (2 Timothy 2:11). In the same way his burial too reaches those who are conformed to his death, who have been crucified with him and have died with him, as Paul has also said: “For we were buried with him through baptism” (Romans 6:4), and we rose with him (compare Colossians 2:12).

As for what is recorded about the burial, the tomb, and the one who buried him, we shall expound it more fittingly and at greater length elsewhere, where these are our chief subject. For now it is enough to mention the clean linen cloth in which the pure body of Jesus had to be wrapped (Matthew 27:59), and the new tomb “which” Joseph “had hewn in the rock” (Matthew 27:60), “where no one had yet lain” (Luke 23:53), or, as John says, “in which no one had yet been placed” (John 19:41). Consider whether the agreement of the three evangelists can move anyone. They took care to record that the tomb was quarried or hewn in rock (Matthew 27:60; Mark 15:46; Luke 23:53), so that whoever examines the meaning of what is written may see something worth reflecting on about these things too, and about the newness of the tomb, which Matthew and John relate, and about no dead body having been there, as Luke and John say.

For he was not like the rest of the dead: even in death he showed signs of life, the water and the blood (John 19:34), and was, if I may call him so, a new kind of corpse. It was right, then, that he should be placed in a new and clean tomb, so that, just as his birth was purer than every birth, because he was born not from intercourse but from a virgin, so his burial too might have purity. This purity is shown through the symbol of his body being laid in a new tomb, one not built of gathered stones with no natural unity, but standing in a single rock, united throughout, quarried and hewn.

The interpretation of these things, and the ascent from what is recorded to have happened to the realities that the events signified, one could expound in a greater and more divine way, setting out such matters more fittingly in a work given to them. As for the literal sense, one might explain it this way too: it was fitting for one who had decided to endure being hung on a stake to keep what followed consistent with that purpose too, so that, having been taken down as a man because he had died as a man, he might also be buried as a man.

Moreover, suppose it had been written in the Gospels that he vanished from the stake at once: Celsus and the unbelievers would have found fault with what was written, and would have brought a charge in this form too, saying: “Why ever did he vanish after the cross, and not contrive this before he suffered?” If, then, having learned from the Gospels that he did not vanish from the stake at once, they think they can find fault with the account for not inventing, as they demanded, that he vanished from the stake at once, but for relating the truth, is it not reasonable that they should also believe in his resurrection? And should they not believe that when he chose, at one time, “the doors being shut,” he “stood in the midst” of the disciples (John 20:19, 26), and at another, having given bread to two of his followers, at once “vanished from their sight” (Luke 24:31), after speaking certain words to them?

choices.why: Restored 'For' (γάρ) at 'For each of them is shown'.
κατὰ τὸν κρίναντα ... ἦν: stiff 'it belonged to him ... in keeping with' -> 'it was fitting for one who had decided ... consistent with that purpose too'.
ἐγκαλεῖν τῷ λόγῳ ... ἱστορήσαντι: 'the word' -> 'the account' (the λόγος here invents or narrates, i.e. the Gospel narrative).

translator_notes: Text: ‘ἐν φιλῇ τῇ λέξει’ is a misprint or OCR slip for ‘ἐν ψιλῇ τῇ λέξει’ (in the bare wording); read as ‘ψιλῇ’. ‘εἰ γὰρ (συν)απεθάνομεν’: the edition supplies ‘συν’ in brackets; read with it, matching 2 Timothy 2:11. Galatians: ‘Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι’ ends Greek verse 2:19 in critical editions but stands at 2:20 in English Bibles; cited as Galatians 2:20. Galatians 6:14: Origen reads ‘τοῦ κυρίου μου’ (my Lord) where the NT text has ‘ἡμῶν’ (our); rendered as Origen quotes. ‘δι᾿ οὗ’ rendered ‘through whom’ (it may also be ‘through which’, the cross). ‘the righteous man says’ (τὸν δίκαιον λέγειν) = Paul in Philippians 3:10; ‘συμμορφιζόμενος’ rendered ‘being conformed’. ‘καὶ συνανέστημεν αὐτῷ’ (and we rose with him) stands outside the quotation marks in the edition; it is Origen’s continuation, echoing Romans 6:4-5 and Colossians 2:12 (‘buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him’); cited with ‘compare’. ‘σκόλοψ’ (stake) is Celsus’s word, kept as ‘stake’; ‘σταυρός’ (cross) is kept as ‘cross’. ‘καθαρὰ σινδών’ (Matthew 27:59) and ‘τὸ καθαρὸν σῶμα’ use the same adjective; rendered ‘clean linen cloth’ and ‘pure body’, and ‘καινῷ καὶ καθαρῷ μνημείῳ’ as ‘new and clean tomb’. Tomb quotations: ‘ὃ ἐλατόμησε τῇ πέτρᾳ’ = Matthew 27:60 (NT ‘ἐν τῇ πέτρᾳ’); ‘οὗ οὐκ ἦν οὔπω οὐδεὶς κείμενος’ = Luke 23:53; ‘ἐν ᾧ οὐδέπω οὐδεὶς ἐτέθη’ = John 19:41 (NT ‘ἦν τεθειμένος’). The ‘three evangelists’ who record the rock-cut tomb are Matthew (27:60), Mark (15:46) and Luke (23:53, ‘λαξευτῷ’); Origen does not name them, so the combined citation sits beside that clause. ‘ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, καινὸν... νεκρόν’ rendered ‘if I may call him so, a new kind of corpse’ (‘kind of’ added only to make the English idiom work; the Greek is ‘a new corpse’). ‘ἔδει’ rendered ‘It was right’. ‘λογάδες λίθοι’ = gathered/unhewn stones. ‘κατὰ τὸν κρίναντα... ἦν’ rendered ‘it belonged to him who had decided’; ‘τῇ ὑποθέσει’ rendered ‘that purpose’. The question ‘Why ever did he vanish after the cross...’ is a hypothetical objection Origen puts in Celsus’s mouth, not a quotation from the True Doctrine; set in double quotation marks as direct speech. ‘ἐγκαλεῖν οἴονται τῷ λόγῳ’: rendered ‘the account’ (the Gospel narrative). The closed doors: John 20:19 and 20:26 both read ‘τῶν θυρῶν κεκλεισμένων’ and ‘ἔστη εἰς τὸ μέσον’ (Origen ‘ἐν μέσῳ’). ‘δυσὶ τῶν γνωρίμων’ rendered ‘two of his followers’ (lit. acquaintances, disciples known to him). The final rhetorical question is split into two English questions; no clause is added: ‘καὶ ὡς βουληθεὶς...’ depends on ‘πιστεῦσαι’, so the second question repeats ‘believe’. Reviewer: in ‘ἐγκαλεῖν οἴονται τῷ λόγῳ’ the λόγος is the subject of ‘μὴ πλασαμένῳ ... ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀληθὲς ἱστορήσαντι’, so it is rendered ‘the account’ rather than ‘the word’.
